differences.title: 1. TRANSPORT LAYER
differences.leftDesc: Relies on TCP for reliable, ordered delivery, but suffers from head-of-line blocking. TCP's retransmissions can stall all streams.
differences.rightDesc: Uses QUIC over UDP, natively handling reliability and order per stream. Eliminates TCP's head-of-line blocking issues for better performance.

differences.title: 2. CONNECTION ESTABLISHMENT
differences.leftDesc: Requires a TCP handshake (1-RTT) and then an TLS handshake (1-RTT), resulting in significant latency before data transfer begins.
differences.rightDesc: Combines transport and TLS handshakes into a single RTT for initial connections, and can achieve 0-RTT for subsequent connections.

differences.title: 3. HEAD-OF-LINE BLOCKING
differences.leftDesc: A lost packet on one stream forces all other multiplexed streams on the same TCP connection to wait for retransmission.
differences.rightDesc: Lost packets only affect the specific stream they belong to. Other streams continue unaffected, dramatically improving resilience to packet loss.

differences.title: 4. CONNECTION MIGRATION
differences.leftDesc: TCP connections are tied to IP addresses and ports. Changing networks (e.g., Wi-Fi to cellular) breaks the connection.
differences.rightDesc: QUIC uses Connection IDs, allowing connections to persist across IP address or port changes, ensuring seamless transitions for mobile users.

differences.title: 5. ENCRYPTION
differences.leftDesc: Relies on TLS 1.2 or higher, which is layered on top of TCP. Encryption is optional and can be negotiated.
differences.rightDesc: TLS 1.3 is built into QUIC. Encryption is mandatory, providing always-on security and improving handshake performance significantly.

differences.title: 6. IMPLEMENTATION COMPLEXITY
differences.leftDesc: TCP and TLS stacks are deeply integrated into the operating system kernel, making updates and experimentation challenging.
differences.rightDesc: QUIC is often implemented in user space, allowing for faster iteration, easier deployment, and more flexible protocol evolution.

differences.title: 7. PERFORMANCE GAINS
differences.leftDesc: Improved performance over HTTP/1.1 but still inherits limitations from TCP, especially in lossy networks.
differences.rightDesc: Substantial improvements in latency, throughput, and resilience, particularly on mobile, high-latency, and lossy networks.
